raw_text:
Transcaval access is a deliberately created, percutaneous, transfemoral-venous route from the inferior vena cava (IVC) into the adjacent infrarenal abdominal aorta, enabling retrograde delivery of large-bore structural-heart devices when conventional iliofemoral arterial access is unsafe or impossible. Its conceptual basis was established in preclinical work showing that a controlled aortocaval tract can be hemodynamically tolerated because arterial bleeding preferentially decompresses into the low-pressure cava rather than the retroperitoneum [1]. The first human TAVR series confirmed feasibility in otherwise ineligible patients, with successful caval-aortic access and closure in all 19 attempted cases and no deaths directly attributable to access [2]. Subsequent CT-planning work defined the essential anatomy: a calcium-free aortic target, close IVC–aorta apposition, absence of interposed bowel or hazardous branch vessels, adequate distance from the renal arteries and aortoiliac bifurcation, and a bailout plan for covered stent placement [3,4].

The technique has evolved from a “last-option” strategy to a reproducible alternative-access platform. Standard transcaval TAVR requires arterial access for aortography, snaring and bailout, right femoral venous access for the valve sheath, and a separate venous site for pacing when needed [5]. An electrified 0.014-inch guidewire is directed from the IVC toward an aortic snare, exchanged for a stiff wire, and used to deliver the TAVR sheath from vein to aorta. Closure is generally performed with an off-label nitinol occluder, deployed sideways against the aortic wall; persistent early aortocaval flow is common but usually benign [5]. Modifications include laser-assisted crossing in heavily calcified targets [6], use through prosthetic aortic grafts [7], sheathless or expandable-sheath strategies in selected anatomies [8], and left-sided venous approaches when right femoral venous access is unavailable [9].

The pivotal prospective NHLBI multicenter study enrolled 100 patients unsuitable for femoral arterial access and poor candidates for transthoracic access. Transcaval access succeeded in 99%, device success was 98%, 30-day survival was 92%, and no patient required emergency open vascular surgery for transcaval complications [10]. Bleeding and vascular complications were not trivial—reflecting the use of permeable occluders, mandated CT surveillance, and very high baseline risk—but the intermediate-term fate of access tracts was reassuring: at 12 months, no late vascular complications were attributed to transcaval access, and most fistulas were occluded on CT [11]. Purpose-built transcaval closure devices were subsequently developed to improve immediate hemostasis, reduce pull-through, and simplify deployment; first-in-human testing demonstrated complete tract closure by 30 days and no transcaval-related major bleeding in a small early-feasibility cohort [12].

Comparative data are observational but increasingly informative. Single-center comparisons suggested broadly similar outcomes between transcaval and subclavian approaches [13], while a contemporary propensity-weighted multicenter analysis found lower stroke/TIA after transcaval than transaxillary TAVR, with similar bleeding and vascular complications [14]. Other institutional and registry studies have reported comparable or shorter length of stay versus surgical alternative access [15]. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses consistently conclude that transcaval TAVR is feasible and clinically competitive with other nonfemoral options, albeit supported by nonrandomized evidence and concentrated expertise [16,17]. A European multicenter registry and more recent niche series—including morbid obesity, transradial secondary access, and left-sided venous access—suggest that the approach can be exported beyond its originating centers when operators follow standardized planning and bailout principles [9,18-20].

Patient selection remains central. Transfemoral arterial TAVR is still preferred whenever safe, as demonstrated by the maturation of TAVR from inoperable and high-risk cohorts to low-risk randomized trials [21-25]. Transcaval is most attractive when iliofemoral arteries are too small, calcified, tortuous, previously stented, occluded, or surgically inaccessible; when transthoracic access is undesirable because of frailty, lung disease, hostile chest, or poor rehabilitation potential; and when supra-aortic access poses concerns about stroke, internal mammary graft compromise, or difficult sheath trajectory [26-29]. Contemporary consensus statements therefore frame transcaval as an important component of the alternative-access armamentarium, best performed at experienced valve centers with CT-planning expertise, electrosurgery familiarity, closure-device proficiency, and immediate covered-stent bailout capability [29,30].

The transcaval concept has also broadened beyond TAVR. Reports describe emergency large-bore mechanical circulatory support, especially Impella 5.0 placement in cardiogenic shock when peripheral arterial access is inadequate or would cause limb ischemia [31,32]. This expansion is relevant to structural-heart programs because temporary support may be required for complex valve or coronary interventions in patients with the same hostile arterial anatomy that precludes transfemoral TAVR. Overall, transcaval access has matured from an ingenious bailout into a specialized percutaneous alternative-access strategy. Its future depends on wider training, dedicated closure technology, prospective comparative studies, and integration into multidisciplinary access algorithms.
